\section[cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere]{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere — to shut in; to conclude, to infer}

\label{lesson:LA-C364-concludo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to throw in the way, then the Latin for to insist.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere}
\textbf{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere} — \textquotedblleft{}to shut in; to conclude, to infer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ex hīs rēbus cōnclūdō eum mentīrī.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{From these facts I conclude that he is lying.}
\end{quote}

\emph{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere, cōnclūsī, cōnclūsum}. Built on \emph{claudō}, to shut: to shut an argument up tight. English \emph{conclude}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{cōnclūdō} is built from \emph{con-} and \emph{claudō} \textquotedblleft{}to shut\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), the vowel changed inside the compound. English \emph{conclude} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to throw in the way, then the Latin for to insist, then say \emph{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To shut in; to conclude, to infer\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis]{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis — a conclusion; the close of a speech}

\label{lesson:LA-C364-conclusio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to insist, then the Latin for to shut in.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis}
\textbf{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}a conclusion; the close of a speech\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Cōnclūsiō tua falsa est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Your conclusion is false.}
\end{quote}

\emph{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis} f. The last step of an argument, and the last part of a speech. English \emph{conclusion}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{cōnclūsiō} is the noun built on \emph{cōnclūdō} \textquotedblleft{}to shut up, to infer\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short). English \emph{conclusion} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to insist, then the Latin for to shut in, then say \emph{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis} again
\end{itemize}

\section[ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī]{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī — to reason, to calculate}

\label{lesson:LA-C364-ratiocinor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to shut in, then the Latin for a conclusion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī}
\textbf{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī} — \textquotedblleft{}to reason, to calculate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Bene ratiōcināris, sed falsum est initium.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{You reason well, but the starting point is false.}
\end{quote}

Deponent: \emph{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī, ratiōcinātus sum}. Built on \emph{ratiō}, reckoning: to work a thing out step by step. English \emph{ratiocination}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ratiōcinor} is built on \emph{ratiō} \textquotedblleft{}a reckoning, reason\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): to keep accounts, then to reason. English \emph{ratiocination} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to shut in, then the Latin for a conclusion, then say \emph{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[significō, significāre]{significō, significāre — to indicate, to mean; to show}

\label{lesson:LA-C364-significo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a conclusion, then the Latin for to reason.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: significō, significāre}
\textbf{significō, significāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to indicate, to mean; to show\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quid hoc verbum significat?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{What does this word mean?}
\end{quote}

\emph{significō, significāre, significāvī, significātum}. Built on \emph{signum}, a sign: to make a sign. English \emph{signify} and \emph{significant}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{significō} is built on \emph{signum} \textquotedblleft{}a sign\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB) and the root of \emph{faciō} \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to make a sign. English \emph{signify} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{significō, significāre}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{significō, significāre}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{significō, significāre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a conclusion, then the Latin for to reason, then say \emph{significō, significāre} again
\end{itemize}

\section[suspīciō, suspīciōnis]{suspīciō, suspīciōnis — a suspicion, a mistrust}

\label{lesson:LA-C364-suspicio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to reason, then the Latin for to indicate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: suspīciō, suspīciōnis}
\textbf{suspīciō, suspīciōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}a suspicion, a mistrust\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
In eum suspīciō cecidit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Suspicion fell on him.}
\end{quote}

\emph{suspīciō, suspīciōnis} f., with a long \emph{ī}; \emph{suspicor}, to suspect, is its verb. English \emph{suspicion}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{suspīciō} comes from \emph{suspiciō} \textquotedblleft{}to look up at; to suspect\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{sub} \textquotedblleft{}up from under\textquotedblright{} and \emph{speciō} \textquotedblleft{}to look\textquotedblright{}: a look from below. English \emph{suspicion} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\section[(dialogue)]{Reasons, causes and conditions}

\label{lesson:LA-R364-review-357-364}



\begin{quote}
Say the Latin for to be of the opinion and to reckon.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to be of the opinion, to reckon, to give an opinion, to suppose, an opinion
  \item to agree, to disagree, to agree together, agreement, a dispute
  \item to weigh, to deliberate, doubt, likely, probable
  \item evident, clear, absurd, foolishness, steadiness
  \item an argument, an example, a lesson, to show, to strengthen
  \item to prove false, to refute, to disprove, to prove wrong, a guess
  \item to grant, to deny flatly, to confess, to throw in the way, to insist
  \item to shut in, a conclusion, to reason, to indicate, a suspicion
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To be of the opinion? (\textbf{arbitror, arbitrārī}.) To reckon? (\textbf{exīstimō, exīstimāre}.) To give an opinion? (\textbf{cēnseō, cēnsēre}.) To suppose? (\textbf{opīnor, opīnārī}.) An opinion? (\textbf{opīniō, opīniōnis}.) To agree? (\textbf{assentior, assentīrī}.) To disagree? (\textbf{dissentiō, dissentīre}.) To agree together? (\textbf{cōnsentiō, cōnsentīre}.) Agreement? (\textbf{cōnsēnsus, cōnsēnsūs}.) A dispute? (\textbf{contrōversia, contrōversiae}.) To weigh? (\textbf{ponderō, ponderāre}.) To deliberate? (\textbf{dēlīberō, dēlīberāre}.) Doubt? (\textbf{dubitātiō, dubitātiōnis}.) Likely? (\textbf{probābilis, probābile}.) Probable? (\textbf{vērisimilis, vērisimile}.) Evident? (\textbf{manifestus, manifesta, manifestum}.) Clear? (\textbf{perspicuus, perspicua, perspicuum}.) Absurd? (\textbf{absurdus, absurda, absurdum}.) Foolishness? (\textbf{stultitia, stultitiae}.) Steadiness? (\textbf{cōnstantia, cōnstantiae}.) An argument? (\textbf{argūmentum, argūmentī}.) An example? (\textbf{exemplum, exemplī}.) A lesson? (\textbf{documentum, documentī}.) To show? (\textbf{dēmōnstrō, dēmōnstrāre}.) To strengthen? (\textbf{cōnfirmō, cōnfirmāre}.) To prove false? (\textbf{refellō, refellere}.) To refute? (\textbf{refūtō, refūtāre}.) To disprove? (\textbf{redarguō, redarguere}.) To prove wrong? (\textbf{convincō, convincere}.) A guess? (\textbf{coniectūra, coniectūrae}.) To grant? (\textbf{concēdō, concēdere}.) To deny flatly? (\textbf{dēnegō, dēnegāre}.) To confess? (\textbf{cōnfiteor, cōnfitērī}.) To throw in the way? (\textbf{obiciō, obicere}.) To insist? (\textbf{contendō, contendere}.) To shut in? (\textbf{cōnclūdō, cōnclūdere}.) A conclusion? (\textbf{cōnclūsiō, cōnclūsiōnis}.) To reason? (\textbf{ratiōcinor, ratiōcinārī}.) To indicate? (\textbf{significō, significāre}.) A suspicion? (\textbf{suspīciō, suspīciōnis}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
